summary: This unit teaches you to manage a project from idea to closure: the business case and charter, scope and change control, the work breakdown structure, scheduling and the critical path, estimating and budgets, risk, stakeholders and communication, leading the team, measuring progress with earned value, public procurement, and closing and reviewing the project.

blocks.p: A **project** is a temporary piece of work with a clear start and end, created to deliver a specific result. Refurbishing a hotel restaurant in six months, launching a new tour route, building a computer laboratory, installing a new licensing system: these are projects. Checking in guests every day and paying salaries every month are **routine operations**, because they repeat without end.

Managers in Jamaican hotels, tourism firms, schools, ministries, agencies and municipal corporations are often asked to lead projects on top of their normal work. This unit gives you the tools to plan them, keep them under control and close them properly.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Show the case for it; write a charter; name the sponsor; identify stakeholders.
Agree what is in and out; break the work down; control change requests and scope creep.
Set dependencies, milestones and a critical path; draw a Gantt chart; deal with float.
Estimate time and cost, including the three-point method and contingency; manage resources.
Keep a risk register; choose responses; distinguish risks from issues; define acceptance criteria.
Use RACI, a communication plan and kick-off; manage a cross-department team and stakeholders.
Measure progress; use earned value, CPI and SPI; report in RAG status; recover from delay.
Follow public procurement rules; plan permits; manage site safety.
Hand over, get sign-off, hold a lessons-learned review and check the benefits.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and calculations (critical path, three-point estimates, contingency, risk scores, CPI, SPI).
A **written paper**: short answers (terms such as Gantt chart, baseline, float, deliverable, triple constraint, RAG) and longer answers.
**Group practical tasks**: planning a small project (charter, work breakdown, Gantt chart, budget, risk register), and running a mid-project review with a change request.

blocks.note: Work every calculation twice. In critical path questions, list all the paths and add them up. In earned value questions, check that you divide the right way round.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Starting a project: the business case, charter, roles and life cycle

flow: Initiation: the idea, business case, charter and sponsor
Planning: scope, schedule, budget, risks, resources, communication
Execution and control: do the work, monitor, report and manage change
Closing: hand over, sign-off, lessons learned, release resources

blocks.p: Phases are done in this order. Control runs alongside execution all the way through.

Before a project is approved, the **business case** shows why it is worth doing: the costs, benefits, risks and options (including doing nothing), with a recommendation. It is the base for the decision to go ahead. It does not list every task or contain the manager's personal reasons.
The **project charter** (or initiation document) **authorises the project** and sets out its aims, scope, sponsor, main constraints and the authority of the project manager. A typical charter holds:

ul: Purpose and objectives, with measures of success.
Scope, and what is **not** included (exclusions).
Main deliverables and key dates.
Budget limit and funding.
Main risks, assumptions and constraints.
Sponsor, project manager and main stakeholders.

blocks.p: Every project is limited by **time, cost and scope** (with quality at the centre). Change one and the others are affected. If the deadline moves a month earlier, the cost, the scope or the quality will probably change. A manager has to decide which constraint is fixed and which can flex, and must tell the sponsor what a change costs.

head: Role
What they do
rows: Senior person who owns the business case and funding, supports the project and takes key decisions
Plans, leads, monitors and reports; makes the project happen day to day
Does the work, often from different departments
Anyone affected by the project or able to affect it: guests, staff, owners, residents, suppliers, funders, regulators
Provides goods or services under contract

blocks.p: Before planning in detail, identify **who the project affects**. A tour company planning a river rafting trip should consult residents and guides early.
A **kick-off meeting** shares the plan, roles and ways of working with the team at the start of execution. It is not a meeting to decide whether the project exists, approve payments or close it.

sections.title: Scope, the work breakdown structure and change control

blocks.p: The **scope** is everything the project will deliver, and what it will not. Write it down and get it agreed at the start so that everyone knows what is included and excluded. A **deliverable** is a product or result that the project must hand over, such as a finished report or a built cabin.

A **WBS** divides the project's work into smaller and smaller parts until each piece can be estimated, assigned and tracked. The lowest level is a **work package**. It breaks down the **work**, not the organisation's job titles, budget months or risks.

flow: Write the final deliverable at the top
Divide it into main parts
Divide each part into smaller pieces
Stop when each work package can be estimated and given to one owner
Check nothing is missing and nothing is counted twice

blocks.p: Example: for a school computer laboratory, main parts might be room preparation, electrical work, furniture, computers and network, software and training, and handover. 'Electrical work' breaks into survey, new circuit, sockets and testing.

**Scope creep** is the slow addition of extra work without changing time, budget or approval, for example the general manager keeps asking for small extra jobs during a lobby upgrade. It causes late and over-budget projects.
Control it with a **change control process**:

flow: Anyone who wants a change submits a written change request
The project manager and team assess the effect on time, cost, quality, risk and resources
The sponsor (or change board) approves, rejects or defers it
If approved, update the scope, schedule, budget and baseline and tell everyone
Keep a change log

blocks.note: When a stakeholder asks for a major new feature halfway through, do not add it at once to please them, refuse without discussion or ask the team to work unpaid. Assess the effect, then seek approval.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A schedule shows what is done, in what order, by when and by whom. Start with the work packages from the WBS, estimate how long each takes, and decide which tasks depend on which.

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: The next task cannot start until the first finishes (the most common)
The stage cannot be built until the site is cleared
Tasks start together or the second starts when the first starts
Painting can start when plastering starts in the next room
Testing finishes when the final installation finishes
Wait 2 days for concrete to cure

blocks.p: A **milestone** is a key point or event, such as approval of the design. It has no duration. A **network (precedence) diagram** shows the order of tasks and how they depend on each other.

The **critical path** is the **longest path** through the network. It sets the shortest time in which the project can finish. A delay to **any task on the critical path delays the whole project**. Tasks not on the critical path have **float** (also called slack): the time a task can be delayed without delaying the project's end date.
Worked example. A food and craft fair has these tasks:

The **critical path** is A–B–D–E, **13 days**. The project cannot finish in less than 13 days. Task C has float: it is on the 6-day path, so it can be delayed by 13 − 6 = **7 days** without delaying the finish. Any delay to B or D delays the fair.

Another check: Task A takes 4 days; B (7 days) and C (3 days) both start after A; D (5 days) starts when B and C are both finished. The longest route is A–B–D = 4 + 7 + 5 = 16 days. C has 4 days of float (7 − 3).

A **Gantt chart** shows tasks as horizontal bars against a timeline, with milestones and dependencies. Use it to plan, to show the team the dates and to compare plan with actual progress. Project software can build it and update it, but it does not replace meetings, the sponsor's decisions or the risk register.

Check that people, equipment and money are available when needed. If two tasks need the same electrician in the same week, **move one task to a free week or find another electrician**. Do not just hope. Use the float of non-critical tasks to smooth resource demands first.
If a critical task is two weeks late, you can add resources or **overlap tasks** (fast tracking) after weighing cost and risk. Do not remove the task, move the end date quietly or stop reporting.
The **three-point (PERT) estimate** uses an optimistic time (O), a most likely time (M) and a pessimistic time (P): **expected time = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6**. The most likely time counts four times.

Worked example: O = 3 days, M = 6 days, P = 15 days. Expected = (3 + 4 × 6 + 15) ÷ 6 = (3 + 24 + 15) ÷ 6 = 42 ÷ 6 = **7 days**. A plain average of the three would be 8, so the formula gives a more realistic figure when the worst case is a long way out.

The most reliable basis for cost is **written quotes from qualified contractors for an agreed design**, supported by past project data. A guess at a meeting, the price of something seen abroad or the money left in this year's budget is not an estimate.

A **contingency** is an amount added to cover risks and uncertainty. It is a percentage of the estimate, agreed with the sponsor. Example: estimate J$6,000,000 plus 8% contingency: 6,000,000 × 8 ÷ 100 = J$480,000, so the approved budget is **J$6,480,000**. Check: 6,000,000 × 1.08 = 6,480,000.

Spread the budget over the schedule to make a **cost baseline**. This is the approved version of the schedule and budget against which progress is measured. Remember to include permits, insurance, training and handover costs, not only construction.

**Procurement** means buying goods and services from outside. In a **public body** (a ministry, agency or municipal corporation), procurement must follow the **procurement rules for public bodies**, which aim at fairness, competition, transparency and value for money. Do not give work to the first contractor who calls, split a large job into small contracts to avoid tendering or pay in full before work starts.

flow: Write a clear specification of what is needed, with sites, timeline, acceptance tests and warranty
Work with the procurement unit to choose the method
Invite and evaluate bids against published criteria
Award, sign a contract with milestones and payments linked to progress
Manage the contractor: meetings, progress reports, inspections
Accept the work against the tests, settle the final payment and close the contract

blocks.note: A public project with a contract worth millions of dollars must follow the procurement rules of the public body. Check the current thresholds and methods with your procurement unit: never guess.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **risk** is something that **might** happen and would affect the project. An **issue** is a problem that **has already happened**. A risk becomes an issue when it occurs, and moves from the risk register to the **issue log**, which records problems with owners and actions.

flow: Identify risks: workshop with the team, experts and stakeholders; lessons from earlier projects
Assess each: likelihood and impact
Rank them by score
Choose a response and an owner
Monitor and review regularly
Update the register when risks change or become issues

blocks.p: A common scale is 1 to 5 for **likelihood** and 1 to 5 for **impact**. **Risk score = likelihood × impact.** Example: likelihood 4, impact 5, score = **20** (a high risk). Likelihood 2 and impact 3 gives 6 (low).

head: Response
Meaning
Example
rows: Change the plan so the risk cannot happen
Hold the outdoor event in the dry season, not in the hurricane months
Take steps to lower likelihood or impact
Train a second guide so one leaving does not stop the tours
Pass the risk to someone else, usually by insurance or contract
Buy insurance against a cruise ship cancelling its port visit
Do nothing now, perhaps with contingency
Minor delays in a non-critical task

blocks.p: Every risk has a named **owner**, so there is someone to watch it and see that the controls happen. The owner is not someone to blame.

Agree **acceptance criteria** at the start: what the deliverable must do for the sponsor to accept it. Test against them before go-live. A new booking system should be tested against the criteria before guests use it. Do not let the supplier decide alone when it is good enough, check quality only when guests complain or skip testing to meet the deadline.

ul: Plan for **permits and approvals** (planning, environmental, building) in the schedule and budget: time, tasks and cost. Do not start building and apply later.

Site safety comes first. If guests are walking close to a crane lift, **stop the lift and fence off the area with clear signs**. Do not ask guests to take care, carry on because they are adults or record it only in the next weekly report.
Keep contractors' safety records and induct everyone on site.

sections.title: Stakeholders, communication and leading the team

blocks.p: List all stakeholders and what each wants from the project and fears about it. Map them by **power** (ability to affect the project) and **interest**.

head: Group
Approach
rows: High power, high interest (such as the sponsor, a strongly opposed community group with the ear of the council)
**Manage closely**: consult, listen and keep informed regularly

blocks.p: A community group that opposes a new attraction near its village and is listened to by the municipal corporation must **never be ignored** because it has no formal role. Meet it, listen, explain, adjust the plan where reasonable and keep it informed.

A **communication plan** sets out **who needs what information, when and how**: audience, content, frequency, method and owner. For example: sponsor, a monthly one-page report; team, a weekly stand-up; community, a monthly meeting; funder, quarterly reports.
A **RACI chart** shows for each task who is **R**esponsible (does it), **A**ccountable (answers for it and approves; one person only), **C**onsulted (gives input) and **I**nformed (told the result).

blocks.h: Leading a team from different departments

ul: You will not be their line manager, so rely on agreement and influence.
At the start, meet each line manager to agree the time each person will give, and confirm in writing.
Hold a **kick-off meeting** to share the aims, plan and why it matters; agree roles with a RACI chart.
Hold regular short progress meetings, keep decisions and actions in writing, and thank people and their managers.
Deal with problems early and in private.

blocks.p: If two team members disagree on a design, **bring them together to weigh the options against the project's aims**. Do not decide by seniority, tell them to stop or remove both from the team.

head: Approach
How it works
Best when
rows: Requirements fixed at the start; design, build, test and launch in order
Scope is clear and stable; fixed contract and date
Short cycles of work; early versions shown to users; changes welcomed
Needs are uncertain or likely to change, such as new software

blocks.p: **Baseline**: the approved version of the schedule and budget. Progress is measured by comparing **work done, cost and dates against the approved plan**, not by how the team feels, how many hours the manager is at the office or waiting until the end.

ul: Percentage complete: 18 of 24 equal tasks done = 18 ÷ 24 × 100 = **75%**.

Spend against progress: if J$3,000,000 of a J$5,000,000 budget is spent (60%) but only 45% of the work is done, the project is spending faster than it is progressing and is likely to overspend if the trend continues.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Value of the work planned to be done by now
Value of the work actually done by now
What has actually been spent on that work
EV ÷ AC. Below 1 = over budget; above 1 = under budget
EV ÷ PV. Below 1 = behind schedule; above 1 = ahead
BAC ÷ CPI: forecast final cost if the trend continues

blocks.p: Worked example. A project has a BAC of J$10,000,000. By now, 40% of the work was planned and 30% is done; J$3,600,000 has been spent.

Check CPI: for every J$1 spent, only about 83 cents of planned work has been done. A CPI of 0.9 with an SPI of 1.1 means over budget but ahead of schedule: the team may be spending extra to go faster.

A short regular **status report** gives progress, cost, schedule, risks, issues, decisions needed and next steps. **RAG** status uses colours: **Green** on track; **Amber** a risk or problem that needs watching; **Red** in trouble and needs action or a decision. Amber does not mean fully spent or approved.

When behind or over budget, find the cause, then consider options with their cost and risk: add resources, overlap tasks, reduce scope by agreement, extend the date or increase the budget through change control. Tell the sponsor early.

sections.title: Closing the project and reviewing benefits

flow: Confirm every deliverable is complete and meets the acceptance criteria
Hand over to the people who will run it, with training, manuals and warranties
Get formal sign-off from the sponsor
Close contracts, check final invoices and settle claims
Close the project accounts and compare final cost with budget
Release team members back to their departments, with thanks and feedback to line managers
Hold a lessons-learned review
Write the closure report and file the records

blocks.p: The **closure report** records what the project delivered against its aims, cost and time. The **lessons-learned review** records what went well and badly so that future projects improve. It is not held to blame a person, to change the aims so they look met or to criticise the sponsor.

Projects exist to deliver benefits: more bookings, lower costs, better service. Some months after go-live, hold a **benefits realisation review**: have the benefits promised in the business case been achieved? Closing the project does not mean the work of the sponsor ends.

ul: Delivered what was promised?
On time and within budget (or approved change)?
Accepted by the sponsor and users?
Benefits achieved?
Lessons recorded and shared?
I can tell a project from routine operations and describe the project life cycle.
I can explain the business case, the charter and the roles of sponsor, manager and stakeholders.
I can describe the triple constraint and what a change to one side does to the others.
I can write a scope and break the work down in a WBS.
I can run change control and stop scope creep.
I can find the critical path and float from a table of tasks and durations.
I can use the three-point estimate and add contingency.
I can build a risk register, score risks and choose avoid, reduce, transfer or accept.
I can tell a risk from an issue.
I can plan stakeholder management, a communication plan and a RACI chart.
I can lead a team from different departments and handle disagreement.
I can calculate PV, EV, CPI, SPI and EAC and explain the result.
I can write a status report with RAG colours.
I can follow public procurement rules, plan permits and keep a site safe.
I can close a project and hold lessons-learned and benefits reviews.

terms: A temporary piece of work with a start and end, to deliver a specific result.
The document that authorises the project and sets its aims, scope and sponsor.
The senior person who owns the business case and funding.
Any person or group affected by the project or able to affect it.
What the project will deliver / the uncontrolled addition of work.
A product or result the project must hand over.
Work breakdown structure: the work divided into smaller parts.
The longest path of tasks, which sets the shortest project time.
The time a task can be delayed without delaying the end date.
A key event or point in the schedule.
The approved schedule and budget against which progress is measured.
An amount added to the estimate to cover risk.
Something that might happen / something that has happened.
Cost / schedule performance index: EV divided by AC / EV divided by PV.
The link between time, cost and scope.
A review of what went well and badly for future projects.

c1.title: A computer laboratory at a St Catherine high school
c1.text: A high school in St Catherine will build a computer laboratory. The principal, Mrs Annette Morgan, owns the funding and the business case. The project manager is the head of ICT, Mr Omar Wilson. Halfway through, the board chairman asks for a robotics room to be added, with no change to the budget or the opening date. The school has not yet agreed in writing what the project includes.

c2.title: A municipal corporation's market refurbishment
c2.text: A municipal corporation's markets department will refurbish a parish market at a cost of about J$22,000,000. Vendors worry about losing their stalls during the work. A contractor is needed. Building permits are required, and the market stays open to the public during the works. A crane will lift roof sections over part of the site.

c3.title: A food and craft fair in Kingston
c3.text: A Kingston group is planning a food and craft fair. Tasks: A book venue, 3 days; B get permits, 5 days, after A; C hire a sound system, 2 days, after A; D print programme, 4 days, after B; E final walk-through, 1 day, after both C and D. For task B the planners' estimates are optimistic 3 days, most likely 5 days and pessimistic 13 days.

c4.title: A community health centre extension in Manchester
c4.text: A community health centre extension in Manchester has a budget at completion of J$10,000,000. At the month-end review, 40% of the work was planned to be done and 30% is complete. The project has spent J$3,600,000. Before work started the cost estimate was J$6,000,000 for the building element, with an 8% contingency.

c5.title: A tourism app for St Mary
c5.text: A parish tourism board is developing a mobile app that lists attractions and bookings in St Mary. The team includes staff from marketing, IT and finance, who report to different managers. A key developer may leave. The rainy season could delay field photography. The app has just gone live, and the board wants to know whether it delivers the benefits promised.

questions.q: What is the main reason the school should have agreed its scope in writing at the start?
o: So the project manager can add work freely at a later date
So everyone knows what is in and what is out
So that the board never needs to approve any changes
So that the budget can be settled after the work begins
questions.why: A written scope sets the boundaries and protects against scope creep. It does not remove the need for approval of changes or for budgeting.

questions.q: The board chairman asks for a robotics room with no change in budget or date. What should Mr Wilson do?
o: Add it at once so that the chairman stays satisfied with the school
Refuse it without discussing it with anyone at the school
Ask the contractors to build it without any extra payment at all
Assess the effect on time, cost and risk, then seek approval
questions.why: Changes go through change control: submit, assess, approve or reject, then update the plan. Adding without assessment is scope creep; refusing without discussion ignores a stakeholder with power.

questions.q: Who is the project sponsor in this case?
o: Mrs Morgan, who owns the case and the funding
Mr Wilson, who manages the project day by day
The board chairman who asked for the extra change
The contractor who builds the new laboratory
questions.why: The sponsor is the senior owner of the business case and funding. The project manager runs the project; the chairman is a stakeholder.

questions.q: Which document would have authorised the laboratory project and set out its aims and scope?
o: A risk register
A lessons-learned report
A project charter
A status report
questions.why: The charter authorises the project and sets aims, scope and the sponsor. The others come later or serve other purposes.

questions.q: How should the contractor for the market work be paid?
o: In full before the work starts, so that materials can be bought
Whenever the contractor sends in a request, with no checks
In stages linked to accepted milestones
Only after the whole market has been open to the public for a month
questions.why: Linking payment to inspected milestones protects public money and keeps the contractor motivated. Advance payment or unchecked requests expose the department to loss.

questions.q: A crane will lift roof sections while shoppers walk near the site. What should the project manager do?
o: Fence off the area, put up signs and stop lifts near people
Ask shoppers to stay alert whenever they pass close by the crane
Allow lifting to continue because the shoppers are all adults
Mention the matter in the next weekly status report to the sponsor
questions.why: Site safety takes priority: segregate the public and control the work. Warnings or later reports do not protect people.

questions.q: How should the department treat the vendors who fear losing their stalls?
o: Ignore them, since they have no formal role in the project work
Send them a copy of the final report after the work is done
Ask the police to keep them away from all of the meetings
Manage them closely: consult, listen and inform them
questions.why: Vendors are high-interest stakeholders who can affect the project. Early consultation reduces conflict and improves the plan.

questions.q: What should the project plan include for the building permits?
o: A decision to start work now and apply for them later on
Time, tasks and cost for approvals before work starts
Only the cost of the building materials and labour
Nothing, since permits are the contractor's own concern alone
questions.why: Approvals take time and money and can stop work if missing. They belong in the schedule and budget from the start.

questions.q: What is the critical path of the fair project and how long is it?
o: A – C – E, 6 days
A – B – C – D – E, 15 days
A – C – D – E, 10 days
A – B – D – E, 13 days
questions.why: The paths are A–B–D–E = 3 + 5 + 4 + 1 = 13 and A–C–E = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The longest path is the critical path.

questions.q: Which one of these tasks could be delayed by 4 days without delaying the fair?
o: B, get the permits for the fair
C, hire the sound system
D, print the programme for the fair
A, book the venue for the fair
questions.why: Task C has 7 days of float, so a 4-day delay is absorbed. A, B and D are on the critical path, so any delay to them moves the finish.

questions.q: The expected time for task B comes out above its most likely time of 5 days. Why?
o: The pessimistic time is much further from 5 than the optimistic
The most likely time is counted only once in the formula used
The formula always adds one extra day to each task estimated
The optimistic estimate is higher than the most likely time
questions.why: The formula weights the most likely time by four, but a long pessimistic tail (13 days against 3) pulls the expected value above 5: (3 + 20 + 13) ÷ 6 = 6 days.

questions.q: Task B slips by 3 days. What is the effect on the fair?
o: It has no effect on the fair, because the project has float
It delays the fair by 7 days, as C has 7 days of float
It delays the fair by 3 days, as B is on the critical path
It delays the fair by 6 days, as the path through C is 6 days
questions.why: B is on the critical path, so any delay moves the finish by the same amount. The 7 days of float belongs to task C, not B.

questions.q: What are the earned value and the planned value at the review?
What is the CPI, and what does it mean?
o: 1.20: the project is under budget
0.75: the project is over budget
0.83: the project is over budget
1.33: the project is ahead of schedule
questions.why: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 3,000,000 ÷ 3,600,000 = 0.83. Below 1 means over budget. 0.75 is the SPI.

questions.q: What is the SPI?
o: 1.33: ahead of schedule
0.75: behind schedule
0.83: behind schedule
0.60: over budget
questions.why: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 3,000,000 ÷ 4,000,000 = 0.75. Below 1 means behind schedule.

questions.q: With the building element at J$6,000,000 plus the 8% contingency, what is its approved budget?
Which risk response is it to train a second developer in case the key developer leaves?
o: Avoid
Reduce
Transfer
Accept
questions.why: Training a second person lowers the impact of the risk if it happens, so it is a reduce response. Avoid would remove the risk; transfer passes it to someone else.

questions.q: The key developer actually resigns. What has happened to the risk?
o: It has become an issue, so it goes on the issue log with an owner
It stays on the risk register unchanged for the rest of the project
It should be removed from all the records and forgotten about
It has been transferred to the sponsor of the whole project
questions.why: A risk is something that might happen. Once it has happened it is an issue and needs actions and an owner.

questions.q: On the app's RACI chart, who should be the one 'A' for the booking feature?
o: Everyone who works on the booking feature of the app
The person who is told the result at the very end
The expert who is asked for advice on the app's design
One person who answers for and approves the work
questions.why: In a RACI chart, Accountable means one person who answers for the task and approves it. Responsible people do the work, consulted people give input and informed people are told.

questions.q: Some months after launch, the board checks whether the bookings and savings promised were achieved. What is this review?
o: A kick-off meeting for the team
A risk assessment of the app
A benefits realisation review
A change control board meeting
questions.why: A benefits realisation review compares results with the benefits promised in the business case after go-live.
